title: Creating Functions
description: Group steps together under a name so you can reuse them whenever you want.

items: Some programs need the same steps again and again.
Copying the lines works, but it gets long fast.
Want to change the wording? You must fix **every** copy, and it's easy to miss one.
content.title: The copy-paste problem

content.value:
print("Go!")
print("Team!")

print("Go!")
print("Team!")

print("Go!")
print("Team!")
content.caption: Cheering for three teams without functions: the same two lines, three times.

content.text: A recipe keeps its steps in one place, under one name. You follow it whenever you need it. A **function** is a group of steps with a name: write the steps once, then just use the name.

content.question: What is the main reason to use a function?
options: To make a program run faster
Write steps once, then reuse them by name
content.explain: A function keeps a group of steps in one place under one name. You reuse the name instead of copying the lines, and a change only needs one edit.

items: Start with the keyword `def`, short for **define**.
Then the function's name, a pair of parentheses `()` and a colon `:`.
The steps go underneath, **indented**, just like the body of a loop.
content.title: Making a function

parts.label: keyword
parts.note: Short for define. It tells Python: a new function starts here.

parts.label: name
parts.note: The name you choose. You will use it later to run the steps.

parts.label: parentheses
parts.note: Every function has them, even when they are empty.

parts.label: colon
parts.note: Says: the indented body comes next.

content.caption: This prints nothing yet. The next section shows why.

items.title: Good names
items.text: Lowercase, words joined by underscores. The name says what it does.

items.title: Not allowed
items.text: Same rules as variable names: no spaces, no starting with a digit.

content.title: Naming a function
content.caption: A name that says what the function does, like `cheer` or `show_score`, saves you reading the body later.

content.question: Which line correctly starts a function named `wave`?
content.explain: You need `def`, the name, parentheses and a colon: `def wave():`.

items: A `def` line does **not** run the steps inside it.
It only teaches Python what the name means. Python puts it aside for later.
To run the steps, **call** the function: write its name followed by `()`.
When the body runs out, Python jumps back to exactly where it left off.
content.title: The surprise

content.value: The tracer below shows the same thing on its own code. Step through it and watch where Python goes.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: The function is defined but never called, so its body never runs. Only the two outside prints happen.
content.code:
def cheer():
    print("Go!")
    print("Team!")

print("Start")
print("End")

items.sub: The steps live in one place.
Every call runs the whole body again.
Edit the body, and every call uses the new version.

content.value:
def cheer():
    print("Go!")
    print("Team!")

cheer()
cheer()
cheer()
content.caption: Same output as the copy-paste version: one definition and three short calls.

items.title: Works
items.text: The `def` comes first, so Python knows the name when the call arrives.

items.title: NameError
items.text: Python reads top to bottom. At the call, the name `cheer` does not exist yet.

content.question: How many lines does this print?
content.explain: Each call runs the whole two-line body. Two calls, two lines each, makes 4.
content.code:
def hi():
    print("Hi")
    print("there")

hi()
hi()

quiz.question: Which keyword defines a new function in Python?
quiz.explain: `def` is short for define. `function`, `create` and `new` are not Python keywords at all.

quiz.question: What does calling a function mean?
options: Telling Python to run the code inside it.
quiz.explain: Calling means running it, and you do it by writing the function's name followed by parentheses.

quiz.question: How many lines does this program print?  def hello():  /  print("Hi")
options: None, because the function is never called
quiz.explain: Defining a function only stores it for later. Without a call like hello() underneath, the print inside never runs.
